Canadian County in brief

Canadian County lies just west of Oklahoma City, with El Reno as the county seat. The April 2020 census counted 154,154 residents, up from 115,541 in 2010, and the towns include Calumet, Mustang, Okarche, Piedmont, Union City, Yukon and El Reno. That growth means a mix of farmhouses and older railroad-era homes in El Reno alongside newer subdivisions on the Oklahoma City side. Commuting to the city matters more to buyers in Yukon, Mustang and Piedmont than in El Reno.

Which offices handle your sale

A sale here touches three offices in El Reno. Value comes from the Assessor, the bill from the Treasurer, and the deed goes through the County Clerk.

  • Assessor: 200 N Choctaw Ave, El Reno, OK 73036.
  • Treasurer: 314 W. Rogers Street, phone (405) 295-6330, mailing address P.O. Box 1095, hours Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • County general line: (405) 295-6000.

Whatever the Assessor certifies on real estate, personal property and public utilities, the Treasurer collects and distributes to the county, cities, towns and schools under levies the Excise Board approves. Overdue city charges for sewer, water, weeds, cleaning, paving and nuisance abatement are also sent to the Treasurer and attach to the real estate account as a lien.

Sellers are often surprised by this. A town's mowing or cleanup bill may surface on the county account months after the city mailed its notice.

Due dates and how to pay

The county uses the state's single billing schedule. Expect a statement near November 1, with half due by December 31 and the remainder before April 1. The Treasurer, at (405) 295-6330, can confirm the exact dates for your account.

Paying through the tax roll website costs a processor fee, which goes to the payment company and not the county. The choices are:

  • Debit card: 1.95 percent of the amount paid.
  • Credit card: 2.75 percent of the amount paid.
  • eCheck: $1.50 flat fee.

Bounced checks carry a $35.00 charge. After December 31 a bill is delinquent, interest accrues at 1.5 percent monthly with no ceiling, and a tax sale becomes possible. Every taxing jurisdiction holds a lien that stays on the land through a sale, so title is not clear until back taxes are paid.

How to protest your valuation

Start with Form OTC 974, the informal protest, within 30 calendar days of the mailing date on your change-of-value notice. Notices typically go out in early April. If yours never came, the window runs from early April into early May.

Steps in a Canadian County valuation protest
StepWhat happens
Informal protestForm OTC 974 and your evidence, sent to 200 N Choctaw Ave or handed in
HearingInformal hearing with the Assessor, held in person or by telephone if requested
Assessor decisionThe Assessor issues a final action within 7 calendar days after the hearing
Formal appealForm OTC 976, filed with the Board of Equalization within 15 calendar days after the final-action notice
Further appealCanadian County district court

After hearing evidence, the Board of Equalization may leave a value alone, fix it or change it, and it sends its ruling by mail. A court appeal is time sensitive, so see a lawyer quickly if you intend one. Addresses and dates shift from year to year.

Homestead exemption and senior freeze

A homestead exemption subtracts $1,000 from your assessed valuation, which the county estimates saves $60 to $114 depending on local millage. You must own and occupy the home on January 1. The deed has to be signed by then and filed with the County Clerk no later than February 1. New applications are due March 15.

  • Additional homestead exemption: a second $1,000 off for a head of household whose gross income last year was $30,000 or less.
  • Senior valuation freeze: for owners who are 65 or older on January 1 and whose gross household income the prior year did not pass $99,000. The application period is January 1 to March 16.

Only the valuation is frozen. Millage can still move, so the bill can change. A state refund on Form 538-H is available to anyone 65 or older or totally disabled with income of $12,000 or less. After a sale the buyer must begin homestead filing in their own name, so the next bill may be higher.

What to gather before you list

Title companies and buyers keep asking for the same paperwork. Pull together your latest tax statement, proof of your homestead exemption, and everything you sent the Assessor, such as a protest and its outcome letter. A printed payoff from the Treasurer makes the title company's job easier, and so does a note of any city charges that were certified to the county.

Because this county has grown quickly, values and bills can shift a lot between years. Did your value just change? Find out whether the protest window is still open before listing. A correction is easier for the owner who knows the house than for the buyer who inherits the number. Take your payoff letter and parcel number to the first meeting with the title company, so closing day holds no surprises.

How the closing handles the tax bill

At the closing table, the title company normally pays any delinquent balance first, then splits the current year between you and the buyer. Expect the settlement statement to show a credit to one side for taxes already paid or owed. If the second half has not yet come due, the buyer usually gets a credit from you for your share of the year. Your job is to give the title company the Treasurer's payoff and the parcel number early, so no one has to guess.

A traditional buyer's lender will also order its own title search and may require delinquent taxes and city charges cleared as a condition of funding. A cash buyer skips that lender layer, which is why a house with a messy tax history can still close quickly.

Selling with taxes owed

Three questions come first: what is the payoff, are there city special assessments, and who owes the current year? Tax is assessed to the owner on January 1, which is why closing agents prorate the bill between buyer and seller.

  1. Phone the Treasurer, or search your parcel on the tax roll site.
  2. Find out if the county has been sent any weed, paving, water or nuisance charges from your town.
  3. Make sure the Assessor has your homestead exemption on file, so the buyer gets a correct record.
  4. With back taxes owed, plan to pay them off, since the lien follows the land.
  5. File away every protest paper, because a final action notice can land close to closing.

Inherited, vacant or in need of repairs? An as-is cash sale can close around a tax balance and skip repair haggling. Every step above still applies.

Frequently asked questions

How do I reach the Canadian County Treasurer?

Visit 314 W. Rogers Street in El Reno (OK 73036) on weekdays between 8:00 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., call (405) 295-6330, or write to P.O. Box 1095.

How fast can my Canadian County value rise?

State law caps annual increases in taxable value, but the cap can reset after a sale or after new improvements. Call the Assessor at 200 N Choctaw Ave for your parcel's details.

When must I protest a Canadian County valuation?

Within 30 calendar days after your change-of-value notice was mailed, using Form OTC 974. With no notice, the window runs from early April to early May.

Who qualifies for the Canadian County senior freeze?

Homeowners 65 or older on January 1 whose prior-year household income is $99,000 or less. The assessed valuation stays put, but the tax bill can still change.

Can I sell in Canadian County while behind on taxes?

Yes, though the tax lien travels with the property and title is not clear until the back taxes are paid. A cash buyer can often settle the balance out of the proceeds at closing.

Tulsa County basics

Tulsa County covers 587 square miles in northeast Oklahoma, with Tulsa as the county seat and largest city. Cities wholly or partly inside it include Bixby, Broken Arrow, Collinsville, Glenpool, Jenks, Owasso, Sand Springs, Sapulpa, Skiatook and Tulsa, plus the towns of Liberty, Lotsee and Sperry. The city your house sits in affects permits and school boundaries, so name the city whenever you ask a county office about an address.

The 2020 census counted 669,279 people and 292,375 housing units, with 8.7% vacant. Owners occupy 57.9% of occupied homes and renters 42.1%. With about 42% of homes rented, many county properties are rentals, and landlords should check whose name the assessor shows as of January 1.

How the Assessor values a home

Each January 1 the assessor assigns a Fair Cash (Market) Value, drawing on sales from the prior 24 months. The office weighs location, size, build quality, condition and age, and every residential parcel gets a fresh value yearly.

Your notice lists three figures. Fair Cash Value is the market guess. Taxable Fair Cash Value is what the tax is calculated from; it may climb no more than 3% a year under a homestead exemption or agricultural use, or 5% on other real property, unless a transfer or improvement is added. Assessed Value (Gross) is now 11% of the taxable figure.

A purchase lifts the cap, so a buyer's first bill can exceed yours. Long-time owners often carry a taxable value far under market.

How to protest your valuation

Step one is an informal protest with the assessor. Unhappy with the result? Take a formal appeal to the Board of Equalization, and after that to District Court.

  • The owner of record on January 1 may protest, as may a representative holding written authorization.
  • The window is 30 calendar days from the date printed on the Notice of Valuation, or up to the first Monday in April when your value stayed the same.
  • Send forms by mail, bring them in, or email informalprotest@tulsacounty.org. Phone hearings are available.
  • Photos, independent appraisals and repair estimates strengthen a case. Sales after January 1 of the current year do not count.

Notices are mailed only when the market or taxable value goes up, so no notice means your value stayed flat or fell. Report storm, flood or fire damage to the assessor at 918-596-5100 and include any insurance or fire marshal report.

Exemptions for homeowners

Six kinds of relief exist: homestead, additional homestead, the senior valuation limitation, the circuit breaker refund, the 100% disabled veteran exemption and religious or charitable exemptions. Four matter most to a typical homeowner.

  • Homestead: takes $1,000 off the assessed valuation of a primary residence. To count this year, file by March 15 or within 30 days of the valuation notice date.
  • Additional homestead: a second $1,000 for homestead owners whose gross household income is $30,000 or less (effective January 1, 2024). Under age 65, you must refile yearly.
  • Senior valuation limitation: freezes taxable value for owners 65 and older who qualify for homestead and fall under the HUD income limit.
  • Circuit breaker (538-H): a refund for qualifying low-income owners, capped at $200, with claims due to the Oklahoma Tax Commission by June 30.

File with the assessor's Taxpayer Services office on the 5th floor of the county headquarters, 218 W. Sixth Street, or online.

Paying the bill

Pay the Treasurer at 218 W. 6th Street, 8th Floor, in Tulsa, or by mail, phone or the county's tax roll site. Half is due ahead of January 1 and the other half ahead of April 1. A bill of $25 or less is due whole before January 1. Late payments add interest, costs and fees.

  • Credit card: 2.35%, with a $1.95 minimum.
  • Debit card: 1.95%.
  • Electronic check: $1.75, up to $100,000.

The payment processor charges those fees, not the county. The Treasurer warns that Doxo.com is not affiliated with the office and should not be used for property tax. Statements go out in November, and remote bank collection sites open for three weeks after Thanksgiving.

Taxes at closing

The county never prorates tax when a house sells. When tax is still owed, the title company can take a share from each side and forward it. When the year's tax is not certified yet and nothing is owing, the buyer normally receives a closing credit for your share and pays the whole bill later.

Unpaid property tax is settled from your sale proceeds by the title company, so a balance does not have to be cleared before you take an offer.

Unpaid taxes and the June auction

Tax left unpaid can send a property to the Treasurer's real estate auction on the second Monday of June; next one is June 14, 2027. A typical year sees 475 to 500 properties sold over unpaid taxes or special assessments like cleaning and mowing.

MonthTreasurer mailing or action
NovemberOriginal tax statements, with a second resale notice if a property is scheduled for auction
JanuaryNew owner and first delinquent statements
MarchFinal notification of tax resale
MayResale publication and land list
JuneJune resale auction
JulyUnsold properties move to the Commissioners' sale list

A statute change effective November 1, 2025 means a property comes off the auction list only if paid before bidding opens. The deadline is 5:00 p.m. on June 11, 2027. Lots that draw no buyer turn into county property, available through the Commissioners' sale process.

Owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled may be exempt from tax resale if they live in a single-family home that is not a rental, earn under the federal income guidelines, and hold an assessor value of $180,000 or less. Apply before each year's resale.

Title and records to check before listing

Deeds and death certificates are recorded with the Tulsa County Clerk, and the assessor updates its records from what the clerk receives. If the assessor shows the wrong owner, the usual causes are an unrecorded deed, an error on a recorded deed, or a lot split that will not show until the next year's roll.

  • A surviving joint tenant on a deed with a right of survivorship clause can file an affidavit with a certified death certificate. Without that clause, talk to an attorney.
  • To split or combine lots inside Tulsa or the unincorporated county, call INCOG at 918-584-7526. Other cities have their own planning offices.
  • A manufactured home sale or move needs an OTC 936 form from the assessor.
  • A parcel is taxed as it existed on January 1, so a lot you sold in part after that date still produces a bill for the whole parcel.

Clear these before listing. Each unresolved item adds time at the title company.

Selling with tax owed

Owing tax does not rule out a quick sale. We pull the Treasurer's record, view the house and write up an offer that already counts the tax and any liens paid at closing. Set it beside the figures for listing. Declining costs you nothing.

Frequently asked questions

When are Tulsa County property taxes due?

At least half must be paid before January 1, and the second half before April 1. Taxes of $25 or less must be paid in full before January 1. Late payments bring interest, costs and fees.

Does Tulsa County prorate taxes when a house sells?

No. The county bills the full year, and the closing company usually divides it between buyer and seller on the closing statement.

How do I protest my Tulsa County value?

File an informal protest with the Assessor within 30 calendar days of the valuation notice, or by the first Monday in April if your value did not change. Call 918-596-5100 or email informalprotest@tulsacounty.org.

What is the Tulsa County tax auction date for 2027?

June 14, 2027, the second Monday of June. Payment to remove a property must be made before the auction starts, with a 5:00 p.m. cutoff on June 11, 2027.

When do I file for the homestead exemption?

Applications are accepted all year, but to count for the current year they must be filed by March 15 or within 30 days of the date on the valuation notice. Later filings take effect the following year.

McClain County at a glance

McClain County lies in south central Oklahoma, just below Norman and Cleveland County, and Purcell is where the courthouse stands. The 2020 head count was 41,662 people living among 16,421 housing units. Roughly 79.8 percent of occupied homes belong to the people living in them, and 7.2 percent of units were empty. Think family houses, subdivisions and acreage rather than a rental-heavy market.

Blanchard, Newcastle and Purcell are the three cities. Byars, Cole, Dibble, Goldsby, Maysville, Rosedale, Washington and Wayne are towns. Three layers go into any McClain County bill: the county itself, the municipality, and the school district. Alex, Asher, Blanchard, Bridge Creek, Dibble, Lindsay, Maysville, Newcastle, Norman, Paoli, Purcell, Stratford, Washington and Wayne all run K-12 systems that levy separately. Drawing a district boundary between two equally priced houses can produce two different annual bills.

Interstate 35 carries most traffic, and drive time to the metro is typically the opening question from a prospective buyer.

Assessor and treasurer

Two courthouse offices share the job. One decides what each parcel is worth and compiles the roll. The other mails statements, accepts money and divides the receipts among the county, the cities and towns, and the schools. Both are in Purcell.

OfficeAddress and contactHours
Assessor121 N. 2nd Ave, Room 206, Purcell, OK 73080, 405-527-35208:00 to 4:30
Treasurer121 N. 2nd, Room 318, Purcell, 405-527-3261, treasurer@mcclaincountyok.gov8:00 to 4:30

If you would rather not drive, oktaxrolls.com has a searchable roll with payment. Beyond valuation, the assessor keeps land records and maps, accepts exemption paperwork, walks every property on a four-year inspection rotation and supports the board that fixes errors on the roll. Use the McClain County Assessor page and the treasurer page for up-to-date office information.

How a tax bill is built

Follow the money in order. Valuations pass from the assessor to the County Equalization Board and on to the State Board of Equalization. Next, the Excise Board certifies millage rates. The assessor then finalizes the roll and delivers it to the treasurer, who mails the statements. One mill is a dollar of tax for each $1,000 of taxable value. Assessment ratios in this state run 10 to 15 percent, and combined mill rates commonly fall between 90 and 110.

Since every taxing body picks its own levy, two neighborhoods rarely match. Read the school district printed on your bill instead of repeating a friend's number to a buyer.

  • Worth of the property: assessor, with a look at each parcel every fourth year.
  • Rates: the taxing bodies, certified by the Excise Board.
  • Statements: treasurer, after the roll is filed.

No first-half delinquency attaches until 30 days after the finished rolls reach the treasurer.

Due dates and penalties

November 1 is when statements become payable. Paying in halves is allowed: one half ahead of January 1 and the other ahead of April 1. Miss that first half and everything is delinquent as of January 1.

  • Small balances, $25 or less, must be settled in a single payment before January 1.
  • Interest on overdue tax accumulates monthly at 1.5 percent, ending when it equals the unpaid amount.
  • Lenders that escrow taxes send one annual payment before the year turns.
  • The treasurer may forgive a penalty or interest if the lateness was not your doing.

Planning to close between November and March? Check with the treasurer whether half has been paid yet. An up-to-date account is simple, and an overdue one calls for a calculated payoff that the settlement agent will want sooner rather than later.

How to appeal your assessment

Send the assessor a written protest. Where the county mailed an increased-value notice, you have 30 calendar days from the postmark date. Where nothing changed, the deadline moves to the first Monday in April.

An informal hearing follows. The assessor must mail a written decision inside 7 calendar days. If the answer is no, 15 calendar days from the decision's mailing date remain to take the matter to the county board of equalization. The form wants valuation information attached, and leaving it off means the assessor's figure is presumed right.

Before filing, collect similar nearby sales, contractor bids for needed repairs and dated photos. Evidence earns a more serious hearing than frustration does.

Homestead exemption and the 3 percent cap

If you live in the house, $1,000 comes off taxable value through the homestead exemption, and assessed value cannot rise more than 3 percent in a year for as long as you hold it. File with the assessor.

A sale starts the clock over. Whoever buys will see a first bill reflecting current value, which can top yours by a noticeable margin, so warn any buyer budgeting from your statement. The break travels with the occupant, so the buyer submits a new application after taking title.

Selling with taxes owed

Money owed on the parcel is deducted from what you receive at settlement. The settlement agent requests a figure from the treasurer. Weeds, cleanup, paving and nuisance abatement charged by a city become a lien on the parcel once delinquent and are certified to the treasurer, so ask whether any exist.

Land with years of unpaid tax eventually goes through the annual delinquent-tax sale, after which the treasurer manages it as county property. Behind on payments, or holding an inherited house with arrears? Find out the exact amount first.

  1. Look the parcel up at oktaxrolls.com and jot down each year carrying a balance.
  2. Call the treasurer for an interest-inclusive amount in writing.
  3. Ask city hall about certified mowing or cleanup bills.
  4. Hand the numbers to the settlement agent so your net proceeds are accurate.

Timeline for a Purcell-area sale

Do the paperwork before a buyer asks for it. At the start, view the parcel record and see which years are open. Within a couple of weeks, ask the assessor whether a homestead filing or a correction is pending on the account. After a contract is signed, the settlement agent orders a payoff of its own, and any city lien shows up then. On the day of closing, the county is paid from your proceeds, so nothing follows the property to the buyer.

An all-cash buyer shortens the schedule because no appraiser or loan underwriter has to weigh in. Clear title is still required, so the tax and lien research is identical. Mention your school district early, since a buyer curious about taxes usually wants schools in the same breath.

Why owners sell here

The usual stories: someone inherited a house, repairs were postponed, a tenant lives in a rental, or taxes went unpaid. About one in five occupied homes in the county has a renter, so landlords are common.

A fast cash sale attracts owners who would rather skip open houses, inspection haggling and a lender's punch list. Condition differs around the county. Rural parcels near the Canadian and Washita rivers, hilly lots out west and older homes in Purcell and Byars each carry distinct repair questions, and an as-is sale hands those to the buyer. Whichever route you pick, get tax and lien amounts in writing first so your net is clear.

When you call anyone about the house, have these on hand: the parcel number, your latest statement, any valuation notice, deed or probate papers for an inherited property, and a plain list of problems you already know about.

Who sets the value of my McClain County home?

The County Assessor sets it. The office is at 121 N. 2nd Ave, Room 206 in Purcell, phone 405-527-3520.

When does McClain County want property tax paid?

Statements are payable November 1. Half has to arrive before January 1 or the full levy goes delinquent, and the remaining half is due before April 1.

What does a late payment cost?

Interest runs at 1.5 percent a month on overdue tax and stops growing once it equals the unpaid tax.

What is my deadline to dispute a value?

Thirty calendar days from the mailing date of an increase notice. If the value stayed put, file by the first Monday in April.

Will back taxes stop me from selling?

No. What you owe comes out of your proceeds at settlement, and the treasurer supplies the amount.

Who bills and collects

Still no statement by the end of November? Phone the office. Each bill stacks county, city or town, and school district levies, so neighbors in different districts can owe quite different amounts.

Due dates and penalties

State law (68 O.S. 2913) lets you pay half or more ahead of January 1 and the remainder ahead of April 1. Fall short of half on the first date and the whole levy goes delinquent on January 1.

For deadlines, the postmark is what counts, with two exceptions: the publication notice and the June resale. A late balance picks up 1.5% a month, assessed on the 16th, and published accounts add fees. When a statement shows BT for back tax, call to learn the real total.

  • Ignoring a statement does not stop the penalty.
  • Publication adds fees.
  • The June resale is the county's sale of delinquent property.

How to appeal your valuation

The first move is an informal protest in writing, sent to the Assessor inside 30 calendar days after the valuation notice was mailed. The Oklahoma Tax Commission's Form 974 covers it, along with 68 O.S. 2876.

  1. Fill in Form 974 with your value opinion and back it with sales, comparables or an appraisal.
  2. A purchase within the last two years goes on the form too, with date and price.
  3. Attend the hearing, in person or on the phone.
  4. The Assessor's written decision comes within seven calendar days.
  5. To go further, use Form 976 and appeal to the county board of equalization within 15 calendar days after the decision is mailed.

If the value is unchanged from the year before, the protest window stays open until the first Monday in April. The board should be done by May 31 or whenever it adjourns. Let the 30 days slide and the Assessor's number holds for the year.

Before closing on a Grady County sale

Get the balance from the Treasurer in writing. It may include back taxes, penalties or published fees. Then make sure nothing else is claimed against the parcel.

The Clerk records the deed: $18 on page one and $2 for every page after. Stamp tax runs $1.50 per thousand dollars of consideration, which matches the $0.75 per $500 in 68 O.S. 3201, once the price tops $100. The Clerk's land records are digital from 1929 on, and a deed handed in by 4 pm is filed the same day.

A seller's timeline

Tax work fits into four stages, and doing it in this order avoids surprises.

  1. Before listing: call the Treasurer for a written balance, and check whether the account carries a BT mark for back tax.
  2. When you have a contract: give the title company the balance and the parcel details. If the house is on acreage, confirm which parts are taxed as farm or pasture land and which as a house lot.
  3. Before closing: ask for an updated payoff good through the closing date, since a penalty of 1.5% per month keeps adding on a late account.
  4. After closing: confirm the deed was recorded with the Clerk, so the next statement goes to the buyer.

If you disagree with your value and the 30 days have not run, filing Form 974 before you list can lower the figure the buyer inherits. It will not change a bill that is already past due, so it works best alongside paying what you owe.

What to ask the Treasurer

A short call answers most questions. Ask what the current total is and whether it includes back taxes or published fees. Ask whether the first half has been paid and whether the second half is still ahead. Ask for the figure in writing, with the date it is good through. If the property was published, ask what the fees are and how they are paid. If a mortgage company has been paying through escrow, ask whether its last payment posted, since lender payments can arrive close to the deadline.

The same office can tell you how to pay from out of state. Card payments by phone and online e-check payments work for owners who live outside Oklahoma, and the courthouse drop box handles anyone passing through Chickasha.

Selling an older or rural house

A typical seller owns either a house older than the 1981 median or a rural tract. Some inherited it. Others live out of state and cannot easily oversee repairs.

  • Roof and system updates a buyer will ask about.
  • Pasture or crop land that is taxed differently from a town lot.
  • Unpaid taxes with a monthly penalty running.
  • Distance from Chickasha services in smaller towns such as Verden, Norge or Ninnekah.

Farm and pasture land can be taxed differently from a town lot, so a seller with a house on acreage should ask the Treasurer and the Assessor how each part of the parcel is classified. Small-town houses in Verden, Norge or Ninnekah are billed by the same Treasurer as Chickasha homes, but the city and school levies on the bill will differ. Knowing which levies apply helps you explain the bill when a buyer asks where the money goes.

Collect the Treasurer's balance and your deed before any buyer calls, and things move faster. A cash buyer can accept the house as is, yet the tax balance still comes out of your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Grady County property tax?

Options are the counter at 326 W Choctaw in Chickasha, the mail, a card payment by phone, the courthouse drop box, or the online tax roll inquiry. The office number is 405-224-5337.

How much is the late penalty in Grady County?

It is 1.5% a month, applied on the 16th, with extra fees once an account is published. Call about any BT statement for the actual total.

How long do I have to protest my Grady County value?

File a written protest with the Assessor inside 30 calendar days of the valuation notice's mailing date. A board of equalization appeal then has 15 calendar days after the Assessor's decision is mailed.

Is a Grady County house worth less because of its age?

The median home here was built in 1981, so age alone does not set value. An older roof or system will matter to buyers, and a Form 974 protest should use sales, comparables or an appraisal.

What if my Grady County tax statement never arrives?

Phone the office if nothing has arrived by the end of November. A lost bill does not stop the deadlines, so ask what is owed before January 1 and April 1.

Muskogee County at a glance

The 2020 Census counted 66,339 residents in 25,525 households and 29,278 housing units, of which 12.8 percent were vacant. Owners live in 64.8 percent of occupied homes and renters in 35.2 percent, so a good share of sales involve landlords, heirs and empty houses.

Property in Fort Gibson, Muskogee and Hilldale schools can carry different levies, so check the district printed on your own statement.

Assessor and treasurer

Two offices handle your tax account. The treasurer answers questions about payoffs and payments, while the assessor answers questions about value and exemptions.

The treasurer's tax roll search lets you look up unpaid taxes by owner name, street address, parcel number or school district. Start with the treasurer's tax roll search or the assessor's tax information page.

How a tax bill is built

Think of the bill as three steps. First the assessor puts a value on the parcel. Then the Excise Board certifies the millage. Last, the treasurer sends a single statement and distributes the receipts to the county, the city or town, and the schools. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value, with assessment ratios between 10 and 15 percent.

Where the owner lives in the house, $1,000 is removed from taxable value and assessed value may climb only 3 percent a year until the home changes hands. A sale wipes out that cap, which is why a buyer can open a bill larger than the one you paid.

Muskogee County also has more than one school district inside its lines, and the levy rides on whichever one your address falls in. Find the district on the statement itself.

  • The assessor supplies value, based on its files and field visits.
  • Each taxing body decides its own levy.
  • You pay the treasurer, either all at once or in two parts.

Due dates and penalties

Statements can be paid starting November 1. The county wants half in hand before January 1, with the rest following before April 1. If the first half does not arrive in time, delinquency covers the whole bill from January 1 on.

How to appeal your assessment

Your protest goes to the assessor in writing. After a notice of higher value, count 30 calendar days from the date it was mailed. With no change in value, the cutoff is the first Monday in April.

An informal hearing is required. If the first date does not work, the assessor must offer at least two more. A written ruling is due within 7 calendar days. Still unhappy? Fifteen calendar days remain to carry the dispute to the county board of equalization. Fill in all the valuation details on the form, because an incomplete protest leaves the assessor's number presumed right.

Pictures of damage, contractor quotes and recent nearby sales give you something concrete to point to.

Selling with taxes owed

Whatever tax is owed gets paid from your proceeds when the sale closes, based on a figure from the treasurer. Cities can also certify liens for weeds, cleanup, paving and nuisance abatement to the county treasurer, so ask for those amounts too.

Steps for selling a tenant-occupied or inherited house

Muskogee County has a lot of rentals and empty houses, so the sale often starts with a situation rather than a plan. A landlord may want out of a house with a tenant on a lease. An heir may live in another state and never have seen the house in years. Both can work through the same short list.

  2. Find out who is on the deed, or whether probate has to finish first.
  3. Gather the lease, keys, repair history and any city notices.
  4. Decide whether to list with an agent or take an as-is cash offer.
  5. Have the settlement agent clear taxes and liens from the proceeds.

Local geography adds a wrinkle. The Arkansas, Verdigris and Grand rivers meet near Muskogee, and the east side of the county rises into the Cookson Hills, so a lot near the water or on a slope can bring drainage and access questions that a buyer will raise. Mention anything you know about both. Taft, home to two state prisons, and Port of Muskogee traffic on the river system round out an economy tied to government jobs, health care and light manufacturing, which tends to keep demand for ordinary houses steady.

Muskogee, Fort Gibson and Haskell each have their own city offices, and a city lien is separate from county tax. Ask the right city whether anything is open on the address.

What sellers here usually face

The people selling are landlords with tenants in place, heirs to older houses in Muskogee and Fort Gibson, and owners who put off repairs. With 35.2 percent of occupied homes rented and 12.8 percent of all units vacant, many houses here are not owner-occupied.

Selling as-is for cash means no staging and no lender repair list. Cash can close without a retail inspection dragging things out, a plus when tenants remain or an estate wants to finish. Whatever offer you consider, ask for taxes and city liens in writing so you know what you will keep.

If tenants occupy the house, tell the buyer up front and bring a copy of the lease. If the house is vacant, expect questions about utilities, break-ins and how long it has sat.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Muskogee County treasurer?

Room 220 at 400 West Broadway in Muskogee. Call 918-682-0811 on weekdays between 8:00 AM and 4:30 PM.

When are Muskogee County property taxes due?

They become payable November 1. Half goes in before January 1 and the other half before April 1.

Does Muskogee County charge fees to pay online?

Yes. The processor charges 1.95 percent on debit cards and 2.75 percent on credit cards, and the treasurer's office does not keep these fees.

How do I protest my property value?

Send a written protest to the assessor within 30 calendar days of an increase notice. No change in value? The deadline is the first Monday in April.

Can I sell a Muskogee County house that has delinquent tax?

Yes. Tax and interest still owing are taken from your proceeds at the closing table.

Oklahoma City, the county seat, sits in this central Oklahoma county, which was formed in 1890 and covers 718 square miles. The 2020 population reached 796,292, among the biggest counts in the state. The towns are Arcadia, Forest Park, Jones, Lake Aluma, Luther, Smith Village, Valley Brook and Woodlawn Park. Because Oklahoma City stretches over 620.79 square miles, a mailing address tells you little about which taxing units apply. The county property search shows the account for a specific parcel.

I-35, I-40 and I-44 cross the core, so buyers usually care about highway access. Hail and wind are the main roof concerns across the area, and a financed sale can slow if a roof carries hail damage or an old insurance claim, since lenders and appraisers ask about condition. A cash purchase as-is does not depend on a lender appraisal.

Who assesses a home and how to contest the value

Values are the job of the County Assessor, whose office is Suite 313 of the building at 320 Robert S. Kerr Avenue, Oklahoma City 73102. If you disagree, the route is a written protest to that same office. Notices of an increase tend to arrive in February, March or April, and each lists market value, taxable value (growth limited to 3 to 5 percent), the assessment percentage and the assessed value.

  • Step one: submit the Oklahoma Tax Commission protest form inside 30 days of the notice's mailing date.

The Board of Equalization meets from the fourth Monday in January until May 31.

Homestead exemption and senior freeze

Homestead status trims $1,000 from assessed value. In dollars, that is roughly $87 to $134 a year, depending on where the house sits. Eligibility means you owned the house and lived in it on January 1, with the deed signed by then and recorded with the County Clerk no later than February 1.

Households whose total income was $30,000 or less can claim a second $1,000. Heads of household who were 65 or older on January 1 and earn no more than the HUD median can request the senior valuation freeze, which locks the value at the taxable figure after that year's adjustments.

The application window opens January 1 and closes March 15, or 30 days after a valuation notice if that falls later. A new deed or a move means filing again. For a seller, that means your exemption stops when you sell, and your buyer starts from scratch.

The deed carries its own cost. Under 68 O.S. Section 3201, Oklahoma applies a documentary stamp tax of 75 cents on each $500 of consideration. Deeds are recorded by the County Clerk, whose website has an e-recording portal and a land records search.

In a county this populous, a listing has plenty of competition. A financed buyer brings an appraiser and an inspector, and either can turn up repair demands. Shingles, gutters, windows and a storm shelter are the usual targets. Needing work leaves you two paths: pay for repairs before listing, or hand the house over as it stands.

As-is tends to fit when taxes are behind, an estate needs closing out, you already moved away, or cash for repairs is simply not there. A direct buyer reviews condition, names a price and takes care of the payoff at closing. Request that number in writing before committing.

Before you call anyone, gather a few items: your parcel number, a recent tax statement, any valuation notice, the deed information and any hail or storm claim paperwork. Having these on the table makes a quote faster and cuts down on back-and-forth with the title company.

The County Assessor, in Suite 313 at 320 Robert S. Kerr Avenue in Oklahoma City. Increase notices tend to arrive February through April.

Thirty days, counted from the notice's mailing date, to file in writing. If the decision disappoints you, the County Board of Equalization is the next stop, within 15 calendar days.

The whole bill or the first half by December 31, then the second half by March 31. A bill left unpaid is delinquent on January 1 and picks up 1.5 percent monthly interest on the 15th.

Woodward averages about 25.6 inches of precipitation and 17.8 inches of snow a year, and tornadoes are part of its history. An EF3 tornado hit the city on April 14, 2012 and killed six people. On April 9, 1947, a tornado about two miles wide crossed Ellis, Woodward and Woods counties and destroyed about 200 city blocks in Woodward. Valuation caps and protests

State law puts a ceiling on how fast taxable value can grow. Homestead and agricultural parcels may rise at most 3% a year. Every other kind of real property may rise 5%. Either ceiling lifts when title transfers or improvements are added.

So a new buyer may pay more than you did. To dispute a value, talk to the county assessor first. A mailed increase notice carries its own deadline, so follow that date. With no notice, you have until early April. Still unhappy? Next stops are the Board of Equalization and district court.

Gather support before you file: photos of damage, repair estimates, and a recent independent appraisal if you have one. A lower value helps a seller only while you own the house, but a clean, resolved protest also keeps the file tidy for the title company.

Settling tax and paperwork at closing

Any tax owed gets settled by the title company at the closing table, and the Treasurer's system lists what is due on the parcel. A mistake on the website does not erase an amount owed, so verify figures by phone.

Tell the clerk if you own a town lot, a farmhouse or acreage, since that helps them find the right record. Ask both offices if anything is flagged on the parcel, before a buyer's title search turns it up.

Plan the sale in order. First verify the owner of record and the tax balance. Second, collect roof, storm and utility records. Third, choose between listing and a written cash offer. After you accept, a title company searches title, gathers the disclosure statement and schedules closing.

When you sign, any mortgage and unpaid tax are paid out of the proceeds and the remainder is yours. With a tornado or hail claim open, get the insurer's position in writing first.

When are Woodward County property taxes due?

The second half of the prior year's taxes is due March 31, and the first half of the current year's taxes is due December 31. Confirm exact dates with the Treasurer, 580-256-7404.

Where do I pay Woodward County property tax?

The Treasurer's office is at 1600 Main, Suite 10, in Woodward, open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays. The site also links to an online lookup and payment page.

How do I apply for an exemption in Woodward County?

Applications go to the County Assessor at 1600 Main, Suite 11. File by mid-March each year to avoid a penalty.

Was Woodward hit by a major tornado?

Yes. An EF3 tornado struck the city on April 14, 2012, killing six people, and an F5 tornado on April 9, 1947 destroyed about 200 city blocks.

Cleveland County at a glance

Cleveland County is in central Oklahoma, with Norman as county seat and the University of Oklahoma there. The April 2020 count was 295,514 residents, and the towns include Etowah, Lexington, Moore, Noble, Slaughterville and Norman. Housing here dates from several different eras depending on the town, so a Moore ranch house and a newer Norman subdivision home will not be assessed alike. Rentals and inherited houses are a common sale in a college county, and both come with their own tax paperwork.

Where to take tax questions

Property tax is handled in the Norman courthouse, 201 S. Jones Ave. Both offices keep weekday hours from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed on holidays.

  • Assessor: Room 120, (405) 366-0230.
  • Treasurer: Suite 100, west side of the courthouse, (405) 366-0217.

Fair market value is decided by the Assessor each year, and a 12 percent assessment ratio applies to both real and personal property. Billing and collecting belong to the Treasurer, who also has a night drop box on the courthouse's north side. If a personal property warrant is overdue, you settle it at the Sheriff's Office, 111 N. Peters Ave., Suite 600.

Ask the Assessor why your value is what it is, and ask the Treasurer what you owe today.

Due dates and the tax calendar

Bills go out in the latter half of November, and you need a postmark or payment before January 1. When the tax tops $25.00 the Treasurer allows two installments: half ahead of January 1 and the remainder ahead of April 1. The first installment has to be at least exactly half.

Interest and fees on unpaid taxes are not the Treasurer's to forgive. Relief, if any, has to come through the Assessor's protest process. You also cannot prepay taxes, with the exception of mobile homes on Form 936R.

Ways to pay and what they cost

Options include the counter, the mail, the drop box and the website. Only the website adds fees, and they go to the processor: 2.3 percent on credit cards, $3.95 on debit cards and $0.75 on electronic checks.

A mobile home paid on Form 936 must use cash, a cashier's check or a money order. Personal checks and credit cards do not work for it.

Homes with an escrow account are usually paid by the mortgage company, and many lenders send the money on the last day of the year. The county's records may take 5 to 7 days to show it. Ask your lender whether escrow has paid before you assume the balance is clear. The county's statement site is taxes.clevelandcountytreasurer.org, and after closing a new buyer can send an address change to CountyTreasurer@ClevelandCountyOK.com so statements arrive in their name. Keep a copy of the last statement paid, since title agents often ask to see it.

Exemptions and freezes

Homestead status takes $1,000 off assessed valuation. The county puts the saving at roughly $75 to $125, depending on location. Qualifying means Oklahoma residency, plus owning and living in the house on January 1, with the deed executed by that date and filed with the County Clerk by February 1.

  • Additional homestead: another $1,000 for a head-of-household owner whose gross household income last calendar year was $30,000 or less.
  • Senior valuation freeze: for a head of household 65 or older before January 1 who owns and occupies the home, with income at or below the HUD median level for the preceding year. There is no yearly reapplication.
  • 100% disabled veteran exemption: removes the full fair cash value of the homestead, on OTC Form 998 with VA documentation.
  • State credit or refund: Form 538-H for owners 65 or older or totally disabled with income of $12,000 or less.

Additional homestead and freeze applications run January 1 to March 15, or within 30 days of a valuation increase notice. Send them to applications@okco14.org or bring them to the Assessor's counter.

How to protest a valuation

The Assessor is the first stop for any valuation complaint. Form 974, the state's informal protest, must be filed in writing within 30 calendar days of the date your valuation notice was mailed.

From April 1 to May 31 the Board of Equalization takes over, and the Assessor appears before it on disputes. Bring the evidence the form asks for: a recent sale of a similar house, an appraisal, photographs of defects or a corrected square footage.

If you lost an appeal, keep the paperwork for your buyer. Protest rights after closing belong to the buyer.

Preparing the house for sale

A short checklist keeps tax questions from slowing an offer. Print your parcel's tax statement from the county site, note which exemptions you hold, and write down what the escrow company has paid so far. If your home is a rental, ask the Treasurer whether any personal property tax is attached to the same name. A buyer's agent in Norman, Moore or Noble will ask these questions early, and a prepared seller answers them without a delay.

If you inherited the property, the tax statement may still list a relative's name. Fix that with the Assessor and the Treasurer before you list, because mail and notices go to the name on file, and an unopened valuation notice can cost you your protest window. Cleveland County mails notices to whoever the Assessor has on record, so keep that address current until the sale closes, and forward anything that arrives afterward to your title agent or the buyer.

Handling the tax bill at closing

Handle the tax balance as a line on the settlement statement, paid out of your proceeds. The county may lien real estate for a tax debt, and no buyer gets clear title until delinquent taxes are cleared.

  1. Get today's balance from the Treasurer or the online tax site.
  2. Find out if your mortgage escrow has paid, and allow 5 to 7 days for it to post.
  3. Make sure no personal property warrant is open under your name at the Sheriff's Office.
  4. Collect proof of each exemption, so the title company and buyer see a tidy record.
  5. After closing, send the Treasurer a change of address.

A vacant, inherited or rental house, or one behind on taxes, can sell for cash without repairs or showings. The same tax steps apply whoever the buyer is.

Payment or a postmark is needed before January 1. If the bill is over $25.00 you may pay half by then and the rest before April 1.

Where is the Cleveland County Treasurer's office?

Suite 100 of the courthouse at 201 S. Jones Ave., Norman, OK 73069, on the west side. Call (405) 366-0217, weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

What are the online payment fees for Cleveland County taxes?

The processor charges 2.3 percent on credit cards, $3.95 on debit cards and $0.75 on electronic checks. These are third-party fees, not county tax.

How much is the Cleveland County homestead exemption?

It removes $1,000 of assessed valuation, worth about $75 to $125 depending on location. Ownership and residence on January 1 are required.

Can I sell a Cleveland County house with back taxes?

Yes. Clear title waits on the delinquent taxes, so the balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing.

Beckham County in brief

Beckham County is in southwestern Oklahoma, with Sayre as county seat. The 2020 population was 22,411, including 11,566 in Elk City, which sits 18 miles northeast of Sayre. The other incorporated towns are Carter, Erick, Sweetwater and Texola. Farming and livestock have long anchored the local economy, and oil has had its boom and bust years. Much of the housing stock is older houses, rural parcels and inherited property, so tax records on those homes deserve a look before you list.

Which office does what

Property tax is split between two Sayre offices, and which one you call depends on the question.

  • Assessor, 301 E Main St. #2, Sayre, OK 73662, (580) 928-3329: why your value is what it is.
  • Treasurer, (580) 928-2589 or Treasurer@beckhamcountyok.gov, mail to P.O. Box 600, Sayre, OK 73662: what you owe and when.

The Assessor does not set rates, write budgets or collect money. Rates come from the local taxing jurisdictions, and the Assessor's website offers a property tax estimator and a school district mill rate lookup. The Treasurer collects and divides all ad valorem tax among the county and its subdivisions, and pursues delinquent accounts through tax sales.

Due dates, penalties and how to pay

Bills come due November 1. Pay everything, or just the first half, by December 31, and the second half by March 31. Any statement of $25 or less has to be paid in one payment.

Beckham County property tax calendar
DateWhat happens
March 15Assessor deadline for homestead and other exemptions and for personal property renditions without penalty
October 1Assessor certifies the tax amounts to be collected
November 1Taxes first become due
Mid-NovemberCurrent statements are mailed

March 31Last day for the second half
Second Monday in JuneTax resale at the Treasurer's office, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

After December 31 a penalty of 1.5 percent per month builds up, and the second half begins to accrue in April. A statement that never reaches you is no defense (O.S. 68 section 2915). Homes with an escrow account get their statement at the lender, which often sends payment in late December, so posting may slip into early January.

Online payment runs through the Treasurer's tax roll page, where a third party adds $1.75 for an eCheck or 2.95 percent of the tax for a card. In person, the courthouse lobby has a drop box at the security desk.

From market value to your bill

The Assessor starts with market value, found through recognized appraisal methods, and multiplies by the state's assessment ratio to get assessed value. Exemptions are subtracted to produce taxable value, and millage is applied to that last number.

Several things feed the estimate:

  • Recent sales and market activity in the area.
  • Size, age, quality and condition of the house.
  • Location and neighborhood influences.
  • Construction type, additions and new building.
  • Comparable properties.

Oklahoma restrains yearly growth in taxable market value to 3 percent for farmland or a home with a homestead exemption, and 5 percent for everything else. A sale or transfer wipes the restraint out. That is why a buyer can inherit a noticeably bigger value than the seller ever paid on.

Protesting a valuation

A protest has to be written, and the Assessor must receive it inside 30 days of the Change of Value Notice mailing. No notice at all? You have until the first Monday in April. On Form 974, the informal protest, state what you think the house is worth and attach evidence such as a sale, comparables or an appraisal.

Let the 30 days slip and the Assessor's number is final for that year. File on time and you get an informal hearing, held by phone or face to face. If that fails, Form 976 takes the dispute to the county board of equalization, and everything wraps up by May 31 or whenever the board adjourns.

Photographs, measurements, sales data and correction details all help. Skip the appeal if closing is days away, but do not ignore a real error, because it will keep following the house.

Homestead exemption

Homestead status trims $1,000 from the assessed valuation of the home you live in. You qualify as an Oklahoma resident occupying the house by January 1. Bring the application to the Assessor's office or mail Form OTC 921 before March 15 each year.

You do not re-file annually as long as you remain and the deed is unchanged. Your buyer starts fresh with their own application. In-person help sessions for exemptions and personal property exist too, so ask the Assessor when the next one is.

Taxes and fees at closing

Deeds above $100 owe documentary stamp tax at $0.75 for each $500 of consideration, minus any liens left on the property. Stamps are purchased from the county clerk at filing. Print the buyer's complete address on the deed. Claiming an exemption means writing the statute reference on it. The clerk can confirm the current rate.

The mortgage tax is its own charge. It falls on a mortgage and never on an ordinary deed. It runs from 2 cents to 10 cents per $100 by term, plus a $10.00 certification fee per mortgage. If your buyer pays cash, none of it applies.

Before you list a Beckham County house

Gather a few papers before the first showing: the latest Change of Value Notice, the newest tax statement, and a note of which half is still unpaid. Check with the Assessor that the homestead exemption is in your name, and ask the Treasurer if the account has a balance. Buyers in Elk City and Sayre alike will want the same few answers: what the taxable value is, what the last bill was, and whether the account is clear.

Inherited the house? Get the deed into the correct name before listing. The tax offices cannot update an account until the transfer is recorded, so an outdated name sends statements to the wrong person. A farm or acreage parcel may also carry agricultural limits on value growth, which a buyer using the land differently should ask about.

Selling with taxes owed

The county can put delinquent property up at the June resale once it has held the tax lien for two full years. Before then, the balance usually comes out of your sale proceeds. Request a payoff from the Treasurer before signing a contract.

  1. Call the Treasurer at (580) 928-2589 for the payoff.
  2. Confirm that your homestead exemption is on file with the Assessor.
  3. Hand the payoff to the title company so it is settled at closing.

A cash buyer can close over a tax balance, which helps when a house has fallen behind. The calendar above covers every seller in the county, town or farm.

Bills are due November 1. The full amount or first half is safe through December 31, and the second half through March 31. Small statements of $25 or less go in one payment.

What does a late payment cost in Beckham County?

Interest-style penalty of 1.5 percent a month starts after December 31 and runs until you pay. For the second half it starts in April.

Where do I send a Beckham County valuation protest?

To the Assessor, in writing, on Form 974. The clock is 30 days from the mailing date of your Change of Value Notice, or the first Monday in April if no notice came.

What does the homestead exemption save in Beckham County?

It lowers the assessed valuation of your primary residence by $1,000. Live in the house by January 1 and apply by March 15.

No. The balance is normally cleared from the proceeds at closing, and a cash buyer can close with it still open. Ask the Treasurer for the payoff first.

McCurtain County at a glance

McCurtain County fills the southeast corner of Oklahoma. Idabel is the seat, and at 1,902 square miles the county is the third largest in the state. The 2020 Census found 30,814 residents scattered across all that ground. Hills of the Ouachita foothills rise in the north, while the south drops to the Red River bottoms. Broken Bow Lake, built in 1968 on the Mountain Fork River, brought a second-home market that sits beside ordinary rural housing.

Broken Bow and Idabel are the cities. Garvin, Haworth, Hochatown, Millerton, Smithville, Valliant and Wright City are towns, and communities such as Battiest, Bethel, Eagletown, Glover, Golden, Pickens, Ringold and Tom dot the countryside. A cabin near Beavers Bend, a farm lot near Valliant and a house in Idabel are three different kinds of property, with their own repair and valuation stories.

No interstate crosses the county. US 70, US 259 and State Highways 3, 4, 37, 87 and 98 do the work, so drive time to a hospital or store weighs heavily on rural parcels.

Schools and weather

K-12 districts here are Battiest, Broken Bow, Eagletown, Haworth, Idabel, Smithville, Valliant and Wright City, with elementary-only districts at Denison, Forest Grove, Glover, Holly Creek and Lukfata. Eight full districts plus five elementary ones means school levies vary a lot from one corner to another, so use the district named on your own statement.

Rain and storms are fair topics for buyers. Smithville averages 55.71 inches of precipitation a year, the most in Oklahoma, and an F5 tornado crossed the county on April 2, 1982. Roof, drainage and foundation condition get extra attention for that reason.

Assessor and treasurer

The assessor appraises real and personal property, figures taxes from fair cash value, checks exemptions and hands the assessment roll to the County Board of Equalization. Afterward the tax roll goes to the treasurer. The Oklahoma Tax Commission audits the office's compliance. The treasurer then pays out receipts to the county, cities, towns and schools under budgets approved by the County Excise Board.

OfficeAddress and contactHours

How a tax bill is built

Fair cash value comes from the assessor and millage is certified by the Excise Board. After that the treasurer sends a single combined statement covering county, city or town, and school levies, then divides the proceeds afterward. A mill means $1 of tax on every $1,000 of taxable value, and Oklahoma assessment ratios run 10 to 15 percent.

  • A primary residence earns a $1,000 homestead deduction from taxable value.
  • Assessed value on that home is capped at a 3 percent annual rise while the owner holds it.
  • The cap starts over for the next owner once the house sells.

The school district printed on your own statement is the number to quote. A neighbor across a district line may pay something quite different.

Due dates and penalties

Statements become payable November 1 under the statewide installment rule. Send half before January 1 and the other half before April 1. If half is missed, the whole levy goes delinquent on January 1.

  • Interest accrues at 1.5 percent monthly and cannot go above the unpaid tax.
  • Balances of $25 or less are due in full before January 1.
  • Mortgage servicers make one annual payment.
  • Treasurers may waive interest when the taxpayer was blameless.

Some websites show other installment dates for McCurtain County. Follow the statewide schedule above, and call the treasurer at 580-286-5128 if a date on your statement looks different.

How to protest your valuation

A written protest goes to the assessor within 30 calendar days after an increase notice is mailed. With an unchanged value, file by the first Monday in April.

The assessor must hold an informal hearing, offering extra dates when you cannot make the first, and must issue a written decision within 7 calendar days. From there, 15 calendar days remain to appeal to the county board of equalization. Acreage and timber tracts draw protests often, because fair cash value on land can vary widely from one tract to the next. Bring sales of similar acreage, a survey if you have one, and notes on road access or flooding.

Selling with taxes owed

Taxes still due are subtracted from your proceeds when the sale settles. Special assessments from a city for weeds, cleaning, paving or nuisance abatement are certified to the treasurer once delinquent, and they attach to the account as a lien. The treasurer also handles county-owned parcels acquired at annual delinquent-tax sales, and with commissioner approval those can be resold. Long-unpaid land does leave private hands.

  1. Search the oktaxrolls.com record, which costs nothing.
  2. Call the treasurer and ask for the total owed, every year included.
  3. Ask the settlement office to confirm there are no city liens.

Out-of-state heirs of land here often struggle most. Working from a real payoff number, rather than guesses, makes every decision easier.

Getting ready to list

Start with the land, not the house. Confirm the acreage on the statement matches what you plan to sell, and note whether the parcel has road frontage. Next, check each tax year on the roll for a balance. If a cabin is used only part of the year, remember that it does not get the homestead deduction, because that benefit applies to a primary home. After that, gather repair facts a buyer will ask about, such as roof age, any storm damage and how the property drains after heavy rain.

With those answers in hand, you can compare a listing, which means waiting for a financed buyer and the repairs a lender may require, against an as-is cash sale that closes on your schedule.

What sellers here usually face

Typical situations include large rural parcels, timber or pasture acreage, older homes needing roofs and cabins used only in season. Many owners inherited the land, or hold a long-vacant house far from where they now live.

A cash buyer purchasing as-is can look past a leaking roof or an overgrown lot and concentrate on the numbers. That helps when repairs would cost more than a retail buyer will tolerate. Before you decide, keep these items together: the parcel number, the latest statement, any valuation notice, and probate or deed papers if the property came through an estate.

If you cannot visit Idabel, nearly everything can be done by phone and online, from the tax roll lookup to the payoff request.

The treasurer's office is at 108 N. Central in Idabel, phone 580-286-5128, open Monday to Friday 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM.

Statements are payable November 1. Pay at least half before January 1 and the rest before April 1 to stay out of delinquency.

Use the View Tax Info and Pay Taxes tab on the treasurer's oktaxrolls.com page, search the owner name and add the bill to your cart.

You get 30 calendar days from the mailing of an increase notice to protest in writing, then 15 days after the assessor's decision to go to the board of equalization.

McIntosh County at a glance

McIntosh County is in east central Oklahoma, with Eufaula as its seat. It covers 712 square miles, and 13 percent of that is water, mostly Eufaula Lake, the largest reservoir wholly inside the state. The 2020 Census counted 18,941 residents and 11,755 housing units. Here is the number sellers should notice: 32.4 percent of those units were vacant. Owners live in 78.6 percent of the occupied homes, and the median age is 49.5, with 26.9 percent of residents 65 or older.

Checotah and Eufaula are the cities. Hanna, Hitchita, Rentiesville, Stidham and Vernon are towns, and Duchess Landing, Shady Grove and Texanna are census-designated places. Interstate 40 and US 69 cross the county, along with US 266, State Highways 9 and 72 and the Indian Nation Turnpike. Most of the county lies inside the Muscogee (Creek) Nation and the far east inside the Cherokee Nation. County property tax is billed the same way in both.

Assessor and treasurer

The assessor values property and files the roll. The treasurer collects. Both jobs follow the state pattern, and you will deal with each at different points in a sale.

How a tax bill is built

After the Excise Board sets millage, the assessor certifies the roll. One combined statement then goes out covering the county, cities and towns, and schools. A mill equals $1 on each $1,000 of taxable value, and assessment ratios across Oklahoma run 10 to 15 percent.

A primary home gets $1,000 knocked off taxable value through the homestead exemption, and its assessed value cannot rise more than 3 percent in a year unless it sells. Lake-area second homes miss out on the homestead deduction, since it covers only a primary residence.

  • Value: assessor.
  • Levies: each taxing body, certified by the Excise Board.
  • Collection: treasurer.

Due dates, interest and new-owner steps

This county asks for half by December 31 and the balance by March 31. Skip that December half and January 1 turns the entire bill delinquent. Only balances above $25 may be split, and no reminder for the second half is mailed to you, so write the March date down.

  • Late tax costs 18 percent yearly, applied as 1.5 percent each month on the 16th.
  • A statement that never reached you is not a legal ground for forgiving interest.
  • New owners should give the assessor a mailing address before September 30, ahead of the date accounts are certified to the treasurer.
  • Mortgage companies often pay through a tax service, so a paid bill can take time to appear.
  • All delinquent years must be paid at the same time. You cannot skip one.

A personal lien on a property can also hold up a mortgage company's payment until the lien is satisfied.

Homestead exemption

Exemption paperwork, homestead included, belongs at the assessor's desk and never the treasurer's. The homestead break takes $1,000 off taxable value, but only for the house where the owner actually lives. A rental or weekend lake cabin is out. Whoever buys and moves in must apply for themselves once the purchase is done, so do not promise a buyer that your exemption transfers. Ask the assessor how a vacant house is classified if yours has been empty.

How to appeal your assessment

Put your objection in writing and deliver it to the assessor. The window is 30 calendar days counted from the mailing date on a notice of higher value, or the first Monday in April when the number is unchanged.

The assessor hears you informally and answers on paper within 7 calendar days. Beyond that you can go to the county board of equalization, with 15 days to do it. The assessor drives by every property on a four-year visual inspection schedule, so a recent drive-by can explain why a value moved. Ask what was observed, and bring photos if the notes are wrong, such as an outbuilding that no longer stands or a roof you replaced.

Selling with taxes owed

Taxes owed are settled at closing out of your sale proceeds, so ask the treasurer for a current payoff. Because all delinquent years have to be paid together, ask for the full list of years rather than just the latest one.

  1. Ask the treasurer for a written payoff that includes every delinquent year.
  2. Ask the assessor to confirm the parcel's mailing address and classification.
  3. Ask the title company to check for liens before you accept a price.
  4. Confirm that a mortgage servicer's tax service actually paid before assuming the bill is cleared.

If you are listing in winter, one more step helps: the treasurer cannot accept a first-half payment after December 31, so find out early whether that half is in.

Selling a lake-area or rural house

Eufaula Lake shaped the local housing market. The lake was finished in 1964 and brought boat building, tourism and retail, and many of the houses buyers look at now are either lake-area homes or older farm and ranch properties. A buyer's lender and insurer will ask about storm damage, the age of the roof and anything that touches the water line, so gather that history before the first showing.

Vacancy is high in this county, so a house that has sat empty is not unusual. Buyers will still ask why. Be ready to explain how long it has been vacant, who has kept the utilities and yard in shape, and whether taxes stayed current while nobody lived there.

Who sells here and why

The usual seller owns an older rural house, a lake-area property, an inherited home or a house that has been empty for a while. With about 27 percent of residents 65 or older, estate sales and downsizing are common reasons.

Lakefront homes, aging rural houses and inherited properties all show up, and many need repairs that a retail buyer's lender would not accept. A cash purchase as-is avoids lender-driven repair demands. If back taxes, a probate or a vacant house is the issue, a straight payoff figure first lets you compare options sensibly. An empty house is also worth a call to the assessor to learn how the parcel is classified.

Keep the parcel number, your latest statement, any valuation notice and the deed or probate papers near the phone whenever you talk to the treasurer, the assessor or a buyer. It saves repeat calls and speeds up an offer.

Land inside tribal jurisdictions can raise parcel-specific questions, so ask the title company about the details of your parcel before you list or sign.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I call about a McIntosh County valuation?

Valuation is the County Assessor's job. Dial 918-689-2611.

When are McIntosh County property taxes due?

Half by December 31, the rest by March 31. Miss the December date and the full bill is delinquent.

What interest does McIntosh County charge on late property tax?

The treasurer adds 1.5 percent on the 16th of every month, equal to 18 percent a year.

Where do I file a homestead exemption?

File it with the County Assessor. The treasurer does not take exemption applications.

Do I need to report a new address after buying?

Yes. Give the assessor your mailing address before September 30, ahead of certification to the treasurer, so the statement finds you.

Craig County in brief

Up in Oklahoma's northeast corner, with Kansas on its northern edge, Craig County has Vinita for a seat and 14,104 residents as of 2020. Bluejacket, Big Cabin, Ketchum, Vinita and Welch are the five towns. One Treasurer bills every house in the county, and only the city and school levies differ from town to town.

A Craig County parcel might be a town lot, a few acres of pasture or a hay field, and each kind has its own tax paperwork. Older homes and rural land are common, and plenty of owners live elsewhere after inheriting from family. Interstate 44 and U.S. Highways 59, 60 and 69 cross the county. Vinita is about sixty miles from Tulsa and sixty from Joplin, Missouri.

Who sends the bill

Two offices split the work: the Assessor sets the value, and the Treasurer collects the tax. What the Assessor certifies on real estate, personal property and public utilities goes to the Treasurer, who passes it along to the county, towns and school districts under budgets set by the Excise Board. The rate on your bill is a blend of several levies, and the Treasurer has no say in it.

Due dates and delinquency

State law (68 O.S. 2913) sets two deadlines. One half is due ahead of January 1 and the other ahead of April 1. If less than half is in by December 31, the full year's levy is delinquent as of January 1. Questions about your own account go to the Treasurer.

  • If no statement reaches you, the deadline stays where it is.
  • An older balance may be noted on the statement, which means the printed figure can understate what you owe.
  • When you owe back taxes, ask for a written total that holds through the day you expect to close.

How to protest a valuation

Disputes start at the Assessor's desk. A written protest is due within 30 calendar days after the valuation notice went out in the mail, under Form 974 and 68 O.S. 2876.

  1. Submit Form 974 with your own opinion of market value.
  2. Support it with proof such as a recent sale, comps or an appraisal.
  3. Take part in the informal hearing, which can be done by phone on request.
  4. The Assessor owes you a written decision inside seven calendar days of the hearing.
  5. Still unhappy? Form 976 goes to the county board of equalization within 15 calendar days of the decision's mailing.

If your value did not move from last year, you may protest until the first Monday in April. The board wraps up by May 31 or its adjournment date. Let the 30 days lapse and the proposed value holds for that tax year. Go by the date on your own notice.

Unpaid city charges on the tax account

If a town's weed, cleanup, paving or nuisance abatement charge goes unpaid, the town certifies it to the County Treasurer, and it becomes a lien on your account.

Vacant or neglected houses in Vinita, Welch, Ketchum, Bluejacket and Big Cabin are the usual cases. Title companies notice an unpaid mowing bill right away, so get a complete account printout from the Treasurer before you list or accept an offer.

The Treasurer also manages property the county acquires at its yearly delinquent tax sales, and may sell it with the Board of County Commissioners' approval. A house far behind on taxes can end up there, so do not wait.

Taxes and paperwork when a house sells

At the closing, the escrow or title company calls the Treasurer for the amount owed and pays any balance from what you receive.

A cash purchase moves fast, since there is no lender underwriting to wait on. Some steps stay no matter who buys:

  • Request a payoff or tax certificate.
  • Clear any special assessment liens.
  • Sign a deed in the form the clerk requires.
  • Pay documentary stamp tax when recording.

Deeds are recorded with the County Clerk, 210 West Delaware Avenue, Suite 103, Vinita, phone 918-256-2507, open 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. The index on okcountyrecords.com reaches back to October 1956. Documentary stamp tax under 68 O.S. 3201 is 75 cents per $500 of consideration, on prices above $100.

A simple order of operations

Sellers in Vinita or out toward Grand Lake can follow one sequence and avoid backtracking. First, call 918-256-2286 and ask the Treasurer for your balance in writing. Second, look at the account for anything beyond the base tax, such as a town's mowing charge. Third, if your valuation looks wrong and the 30 days have not run, file Form 974 before you list, since a lower value helps the next owner too. Fourth, ask the County Clerk at 918-256-2507 how your deed should be formatted. Finally, hand the title company the Treasurer's total and the Clerk's requirements so the closing date holds.

If you own near Grand Lake O' the Cherokees and live elsewhere, mail may go to an address nobody checks. Confirm with the Treasurer that statements reach you, because an unread bill carries the same penalty as a read one. Having the account printout in hand when you list a Vinita house, whether on Historic U.S. 66 or closer to Interstate 44, answers a buyer's first tax question before it is asked.

Out in Welch, Ketchum or along U.S. 69 near Big Cabin, the parcel is often acreage. Know its size and legal description before you list, and copy both from your last recorded deed so the listing, the tax account and the new deed all agree.

A plain sale rarely needs a lawyer, though probate or a split among heirs may. A short call to the offices above usually settles which papers you need.

What Craig County sellers usually run into

Three things cause most of the trouble here: age, distance and paperwork.

  • Inherited houses whose heirs live in several states.
  • Rural lots whose legal descriptions involve acreage and mineral questions.
  • Lake-area properties tied to Grand Lake, which the Pensacola Dam created.
  • Houses with unpaid city charges or back taxes on the account.

Whatever your situation, begin with the Treasurer's balance and the Clerk's records. That way the last week before closing stays calm.

With several heirs, decide early who signs the deed and who covers the tax balance. Collect the death certificate, the probate papers and the latest tax statement, so the title company can confirm the right people may sell. Ask the Clerk what a recordable deed looks like here, since one that misses the format comes back and can delay closing. A cash buyer may take the house as is, yet the taxes and city liens still come out of the proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

Who handles property tax bills in Craig County, Oklahoma?

For a bill or a payment, phone the Treasurer at 918-256-2286 or stop by Suite 104 at 210 W. Delaware in Vinita on a weekday. Questions about what your house is valued at go to the Assessor in the courthouse.

How long do I have to protest a Craig County valuation?

Thirty calendar days, counted from the mailing date of the valuation notice, and the protest goes to the Assessor in writing. A value that did not change from last year can be protested until the first Monday in April.

When do Craig County taxes become delinquent?

They go delinquent on January 1 if half has not been paid by then. The second half has until April 1.

Can I sell a Craig County house with taxes still owed?

Yes, and the balance is normally paid out of your proceeds at closing. Start with a written total from the Treasurer, and resolve any special assessments the city sent to the county.

What stamp tax applies to a Craig County deed?

The rate is 75 cents per $500 of consideration under 68 O.S. 3201, owed on prices above $100 when the deed is recorded.
